title: Mathematics AI HL - Set B - Paper 2

questions.stem: A community centre can buy an energy system for \$18000 now. It produces savings of \$3200 at the end of year 1; these savings increase by $3\%$ each year for eight years. Maintenance of \$900 is paid at the end of each year. A resale receipt of \$2000 is received at the end of year 8 in addition to that year's savings. All amounts quoted are nominal cash flows. Define net present value as discounted receipts minus discounted payments.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Build a correctly timed cash-flow model and distinguish discount rate, IRR and inflation-adjusted growth.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write an expression for the net present value $V(r)$ when the effective annual discount rate is $r$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the net present value at $r=0.06$, to the nearest dollar, and interpret its sign.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The internal rate of return is the positive value of $r$ for which $V(r)=0$. Find it as a percentage. Explain why there is at most one positive solution for these cash flows.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Annual inflation is $2\%$. Find the annual growth rate in the purchasing power of the gross savings.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: An alternative system costs the same initially and gives a guaranteed net receipt of \$2600 at the end of each of nine years, with no resale value. Compare the two systems using a $6\%$ discount rate.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: State two distinct forecasting risks in the first system which the NPV calculation does not remove.

steps.text: The net annual saving in year $j$ is $3200(1.03)^{j-1}-900$.
Discount each year-end flow by $(1+r)^j$.
Include $2000/(1+r)^8$ for the additional resale receipt.
$V(0.06)=-444.6266$ dollars, giving $-445$ dollars to the nearest dollar.
The negative value means the investment does not meet a $6\%$ effective annual required return under these forecasts.
Solve the stated NPV equation numerically for $r>0$.
Every future net receipt is positive.
Each discounted positive receipt decreases as $r$ increases, so $V$ is strictly decreasing for $r>0$.
Divide the nominal savings growth factor by the inflation growth factor.
The real growth factor is $1.03/1.02$.
The real growth rate is $0.9803922\%$ per year.
For the alternative, calculate $-18000+\sum_{j=1}^{9}2600/(1.06)^j$.
The alternative NPV is $-315.6001$ dollars.
Compare this value with $-444.6266$ for the first system; choose the higher NPV if one must be selected. A negative NPV still fails the required return.
The actual future savings or their growth may differ from the forecast, for example because energy prices change.
Maintenance, service life or resale value may differ; discounting does not guarantee these uncertain cash flows.

questions.answerSummary: $V(r)=-18000+\sum_{j=1}^{8}\{3200(1.03)^{j-1}-900\}/(1+r)^j+2000/(1+r)^8$.; The negative value means the investment does not meet a $6\%$ effective annual required return under these forecasts.; Each discounted positive receipt decreases as $r$ increases, so $V$ is strictly decreasing for $r>0$.; The real growth rate is $0.9803922\%$ per year.; Compare this value with $-444.6266$ for the first system; choose the higher NPV if one must be selected. A negative NPV still fails the required return.; Maintenance, service life or resale value may differ; discounting does not guarantee these uncertain cash flows.

questions.stem: Three service centres have coordinates $A(2,2)$, $B(10,2)$ and $C(6,8)$, in kilometres. Their service region is the rectangle $0\le x\le12$, $0\le y\le10$. Initially each location is allocated to its nearest centre by straight-line distance. The sites are shown on the diagram.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Connect bisector equations, bounded-cell geometry and the difference between distance and travel-time models.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ and the point where the three Voronoi boundaries meet. Verify that this point is also equidistant from $B$ and $C$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the area of the Voronoi cell allocated to $A$ within the rectangular region.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Within the cell for $A$, locate the point farthest from $A$ and find its distance. You may use the fact that the maximum distance from a fixed point over a convex polygon is attained at a vertex.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: At $D(5,4)$, straight-line response speeds from $A,B,C$ are respectively $40,80,30$ km per hour. Determine the fastest centre and explain why this may differ from the Voronoi allocation.

steps.text: $AB$ is horizontal with midpoint $(6,2)$.
The bisector is $x=6$.
The bisector is $2x+3y=23$.
Intersect this with $x=6$.
The common vertex is $(6,11/3)$.
The $BC$ bisector is $-2x+3y=-1$, satisfied by the same point.
The cell satisfies $x\le6$ and $2x+3y\le23$, with the rectangle bounds.
Use a trapezium area or integrate the upper edge from $x=0$ to $6$.
The area is $34\ \mathrm{km}^2$.
Compare distances from $A$ to the four cell vertices.
The squared distances are $8,20,169/9,325/9$, respectively.
The farthest vertex is $(0,23/3)$.
The maximum distance is $\sqrt{325}/3=6.009252$ km.
Distances from $D$ to $A,B,C$ are $\sqrt{13},\sqrt{29},\sqrt{17}$ km; divide by the respective speeds.
Times are $5.408327$, $4.038874$ and $8.246211$ minutes, so $B$ is fastest.
Distance-only allocation gives $A$, but unequal speeds mean nearest distance need not minimize response time.

questions.answerSummary: The bisector is $x=6$.; The $BC$ bisector is $-2x+3y=-1$, satisfied by the same point.; The area is $34\ \mathrm{km}^2$.; The maximum distance is $\sqrt{325}/3=6.009252$ km.; Distance-only allocation gives $A$, but unequal speeds mean nearest distance need not minimize response time.

questions.stem: In a clinic, hourly counts of appointments and walk-ins are independent Poisson variables with means $2.4$ and $3.6$. Thus the total hourly count $N$ is Poisson with mean $6$. Counts in disjoint time intervals are independent, with constant rates. In parts (d) and (e), use one-tailed tests for an increase in the total arrival rate.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Handle count tails and conditional allocation exactly; separate significance, discrete rejection region and power.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the probability of at least ten arrivals in one hour.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Given that there are five arrivals in an hour, the number of appointments has a binomial distribution. Find its success probability and calculate the probability that at least three of the five are appointments.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A two-hour session has capacity for $m$ arrivals. Find the smallest integer $m$ for which the probability of arrivals exceeding capacity is less than $0.01$. Show the adjacent probabilities used.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: In eight observed hours there are $65$ arrivals. Test at the $5\%$ level whether the hourly total rate has increased from $6$. State hypotheses, distribution and conclusion.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: For the same eight-hour test, find the rejection region with the largest Type I error probability strictly below $0.05$. Then calculate and interpret the probability of a Type II error if the true hourly rate is $7$.

steps.text: $P(N\ge10)=1-P(N\le9)$, with $N\sim\operatorname{Po}(6)$.
Use the Poisson cumulative probability with upper included count $9$.
The probability is $0.08392402$.
The appointment fraction is $2.4/(2.4+3.6)=0.4$.
The conditional count is $\operatorname{Bin}(5,0.4)$.
Use $1-P(X\le2)$.
The conditional probability is $0.31744$.
The two-hour count is $\operatorname{Po}(12)$; require $P(N>m)<0.01$.
At $m=21$ the tail is $0.006065147$; at one less it is $0.01159774$.
The smallest capacity is $21$.
$H_0:\lambda=6$ per hour, $H_1:\lambda>6$ per hour.
Under $H_0$, the eight-hour count is $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(48)$.
Reject $H_0$ since $p<0.05$; the observed count supports an increased rate.
Find the smallest integer $k$ with $P(\operatorname{Po}(48)\ge k)<0.05$.
Reject for $X\ge61$; the actual Type I error probability is $0.03950011$.
At rate $7$, the eight-hour count is $\operatorname{Po}(56)$; a Type II error is $X<61$.
The Type II probability is $0.7309104$.
This is the probability that the test fails to detect an increase when the true hourly rate is $7$, not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

questions.answerSummary: The probability is $0.08392402$.; The conditional probability is $0.31744$.; The smallest capacity is $21$.; Reject $H_0$ since $p<0.05$; the observed count supports an increased rate.; This is the probability that the test fails to detect an increase when the true hourly rate is $7$, not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

questions.stem: A learning website has pages $A,B,C$. Each minute a visitor either stays or follows one link. Using column state vectors, the transition matrix is $T=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.2&0.1\\0.3&0.5&0.3\\0.1&0.3&0.6\end{pmatrix}$, where $T_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from page $j$ to page $i$. Initially $1000$ visitors are all on $A$. Each visitor remains in the model and evolves independently. Repeated visits to $C$ in different minutes are counted separately.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Use the declared column convention, distinguish occupancy from visits, and compare a revised navigation policy.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the probability of moving from $B$ to $C$ in one minute and find the expected state vector after one minute.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the expected numbers on each page after two minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the steady-state proportions on the three pages. Show the equations and normalization used.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why the steady state is approached from any initial probability distribution.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Find the expected total number of visits to $C$ during minutes $1,2,3,4,5$ by the $1000$ visitors.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: An additional link changes the probabilities from page $C$ to $(0.25,0.30,0.45)^T$, leaving the other columns unchanged. Find the new steady state and assess whether this increases the long-run fraction on $C$.

steps.text: The probability from $B$ to $C$ is the row $C$, column $B$ entry, $0.3$.
The expected counts are $(600,300,100)^T$.
The probability vector is $(0.43,0.36,0.21)^T$.
The expected counts are $(430,360,210)^T$.
Solve $T\mathbf s=\mathbf s$.
For example, $0.4a=0.2b+0.1c$ and $0.5b=0.3a+0.3c$.
Add $a+b+c=1$ to give a unique normalized state.
The steady state is $(0.275,0.375,0.35)^T$.
These are long-run fractions, and multiplying by $1000$ gives the corresponding limiting expected counts.
Every entry of $T$ is strictly positive, so the transition matrix is regular.
A regular Markov chain approaches its unique steady-state distribution independently of its initial distribution.
For one visitor initially on $A$, use the $C$ component of $T^n(1,0,0)^T$ in minute $n$.
Add those five probabilities, rather than using only the minute-5 occupancy.
The expected visits per visitor total $1.23123$.
The expected aggregate is $1231.23$ visits; repeated visits are included.
Replace the third column and solve $T_{\rm new}\mathbf s=\mathbf s$, $a+b+c=1$.
The new proportions are $(0.3557692,0.375,0.2692308)^T$.
The fraction on $C$ decreases from $0.35$ to $0.2692308$, so the change does not meet that objective.

questions.answerSummary: The expected counts are $(600,300,100)^T$.; The expected counts are $(430,360,210)^T$.; These are long-run fractions, and multiplying by $1000$ gives the corresponding limiting expected counts.; A regular Markov chain approaches its unique steady-state distribution independently of its initial distribution.; The expected aggregate is $1231.23$ visits; repeated visits are included.; The fraction on $C$ decreases from $0.35$ to $0.2692308$, so the change does not meet that objective.

questions.stem:
A vehicle is tested on one dry road. Speed $v$ is in km per hour and braking distance $d$ is in metres. Use a power model $d=kv^b$, fitted by linear regression of $\ln d$ on $\ln v$.

| $v$ | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 70 | 80 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $d$ | 3.2 | 6.9 | 12.6 | 20.1 | 29.5 | 39.8 | 53.0 |
questions.cognitiveDemand: Linearize a power relation, retain units in a stopping model and solve an implicit safety design limit.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find $k$ and $b$, and the correlation coefficient for the linearized data.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the model to predict the braking distance at $65$ km per hour and find the residual at $80$ km per hour, taking residual as observed minus predicted distance.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The driver's reaction time is $1.1$ seconds. Find the largest speed for which the modelled total stopping distance is at most $50$ metres. Show the equation solved and justify choosing the boundary solution.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: An alert system reduces reaction time to $0.85$ seconds without changing braking performance. Find the new largest speed for the same $50$-metre stopping distance and explain why the braking coefficient $k$ is unchanged.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why the high linearized correlation does not justify using this model on an icy road at $120$ km per hour. State what quantity the log-linear regression minimizes.

steps.text: Fit $\ln d=a+b\ln v$.
The correlation coefficient of the log data is $r=0.9998259$.
Substitute the speeds into $kv^b$, using unrounded regression coefficients.
The prediction at $65$ is $34.34158$ m.
The speed in metres per second is $v/3.6$, so total stopping distance is $1.1v/3.6+kv^b$.
Solve $1.1v/3.6+kv^b=50$ on the tested speed interval.
The boundary speed is $61.89802$ km per hour.
Both terms increase for $v>0$ since $k,b>0$, so this is the largest admissible speed.
Replace only the reaction term: $0.85v/3.6+kv^b=50$.
The new boundary speed is $65.23683$ km per hour.
The system changes reaction time, not the measured relationship between speed and braking distance.
Therefore the original braking regression and its coefficient $k$ remain in the model.
The road condition differs from that of the measurements, so the same braking parameters need not apply.
$120$ lies outside the observed speed range, making this an extrapolation.
The fitted line minimizes the sum of squared residuals in $\ln d$, not in the original distances $d$.

questions.answerSummary: The correlation coefficient of the log data is $r=0.9998259$.; At $80$, the residual is $53-52.41465=0.5853497$ m.; Both terms increase for $v>0$ since $k,b>0$, so this is the largest admissible speed.; Therefore the original braking regression and its coefficient $k$ remain in the model.; The fitted line minimizes the sum of squared residuals in $\ln d$, not in the original distances $d$.

questions.stem: A managed culture is modelled by $N(t)=\dfrac{1200}{1+11e^{-0.42t}}$, where $N$ is the expected number of organisms and $t\ge0$ is time in days. A proposed differential model is $N\prime=rN(1-N/1200)$. Resource conditions are held fixed during the observation period.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Connect explicit and differential logistic forms and distinguish maximum instantaneous growth from mean population.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the initial population and limiting population, and interpret the constant $1200$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Differentiate $N(t)$ and show that the proposed differential model holds for a particular value of $r$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the largest instantaneous growth rate and the time at which it occurs. Justify that it is a maximum.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find the mean population over days $5$ to $10$. Explain why this need not equal the population on day $7.5$.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why this model predicts no overshoot above $1200$ from the stated initial condition. Give one plausible change to the real culture which would invalidate the fixed carrying-capacity assumption.

steps.text: $N(t)$ approaches $1200$ as $t$ increases.
$1200$ is the modelled carrying capacity under the fixed resource conditions.
Apply the chain rule to $1200(1+11e^{-0.42t})^{-1}$.
The expressions agree for $r=0.42$ per day.
Treat growth as $G(N)=0.42N(1-N/1200)$.
This downward-opening quadratic is maximized at $N=600$.
The maximum rate is $126$ organisms per day.
The time mean is $\frac15\int_5^{10}N(t)\,dt$.
The mean is $799.7329$ organisms.
The midpoint population is $N(7.5)=815.5646$.
For a nonlinear function, an interval average generally differs from the value at the midpoint; they answer different questions.
The denominator is $1+11e^{-0.42t}>1$ for every finite $t\ge0$, so $N(t)<1200$.
Also $N\prime>0$ while $0<N<1200$, with growth tending to zero near capacity.
A change in nutrient supply, available space, temperature or waste accumulation could change the effective carrying capacity.

questions.answerSummary: $1200$ is the modelled carrying capacity under the fixed resource conditions.; The expressions agree for $r=0.42$ per day.; $11e^{-0.42t}=1$, giving $t=5.709274$ days.; For a nonlinear function, an interval average generally differs from the value at the midpoint; they answer different questions.; A change in nutrient supply, available space, temperature or waste accumulation could change the effective carrying capacity.
